short_title: DOF-RIPS v. Office of the Ombudsman (Gomez)
full_title: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE-REVENUE INTEGRITY PROTECTION SERVICE (DOF-RIPS), REPRESENTED BY JOEL M. APOLONIO AND AGAPITO C. GUARIN, PETITIONER, VS. OFFICE OF THE OMBUDSMAN AND RAMIR SAUNDERS GOMEZ, SPECIAL AGENT I, BUREAU OF CUSTOMS, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: II. The Revised Penal Code – Book One > D. Extinction of Criminal Liability > 1. Total Extinction > e. Prescription > ii. Prescription under Special Laws (Act 3326)
topics: Section 8 of RA 6713 expressly amended Section 7 of RA 3019 on non-filing of SALN (Sec. 16, RA 6713)
Non-filing of SALN prescribes in eight years under Act No. 3326
Perjury in a SALN prescribes in ten years, reckoned from filing of the SALN
Judicial non-interference with the Ombudsman's prosecutorial findings absent grave abuse of discretion

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 4. The Ombudsman and the Special Prosecutor (RA 6770) > d. Judicial Review

doctrine:
**Section 8 of RA 6713 amended Section 7 of RA 3019 on the non-filing of the SALN, through the express repealing clause in Section 16 of RA 6713.** Section 16 repeals or modifies inconsistent laws "unless the same provide for a heavier penalty." RA 6713 imposes the heavier penalty: imprisonment not exceeding five years, a fine not exceeding P5,000, or both, plus disqualification from public office. RA 3019 imposes only a fine of P100 to P1,000, imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both. Because the repeal is express, the rule against implied repeals does not apply. **A public officer cannot be indicted for the same non-filing under both laws; he may be prosecuted only under RA 6713.**

RA 6713 sets no prescriptive period, so Act No. 3326 governs. **A violation of Section 8 of RA 6713 prescribes in eight years** (Act No. 3326, Sec. 1(c): imprisonment of two years or more but less than six years). The 15-year period for RA 3019 offenses under BP 195 does not apply. This reiterates Del Rosario v. People, DOF-RIPS v. Ombudsman (Casayuran), and DOF-RIPS v. Ombudsman (Germar).

**Perjury (Art. 183, RPC) committed through false statements in a SALN prescribes in ten years (Art. 90), reckoned from the filing of the SALN**, not from the complainant's later discovery of the falsity (reiterating Germar). Perjury is consummated upon filing, and the SALN is then open to review. This harmonizes Article 91 of the RPC with Section 8(C)(4) of RA 6713, which keeps SALNs available to the public for ten years. The Court applied the same reckoning to the falsification charges based on the same SALN entries. The Court also reiterated that it does not interfere with the Ombudsman's investigatory and prosecutorial findings unless grave abuse of discretion is shown; mere disagreement is not enough.
facts:
On August 28, 2015, the DOF-Revenue Integrity Protection Service (DOF-RIPS) filed a complaint with the Office of the Ombudsman against Ramir Saunders Gomez, Special Agent I of the Bureau of Customs. The complaint charged violations of RA 3019, RA 6713, and Articles 171(4) and 183 of the RPC. It alleged that Gomez failed to file his 2003 SALN. It also alleged that he did not disclose six lots in Old Cabalan, Olongapo City in his SALNs for 1996 to 2009 (titles issued in his name in 1996 and 1998), a townhouse in Quezon City in his SALNs for 2004 to 2008, a Toyota Revo in his 2005 SALN, and a 9mm pistol in his SALNs for 2010 to 2013. Finally, it alleged that he filed inconsistent 2006 SALNs with false declarations. Gomez denied the charges, blamed his bookkeeper, and gave explanations for each item.

In a Resolution dated June 23, 2017, the Ombudsman found probable cause for three counts of perjury and three counts of falsification covering his 2007, 2008, and 2009 SALNs. It held that the non-filing of the 2003 SALN was punishable only under RA 6713, because RA 6713 has the heavier penalty and modified RA 3019, and that it had prescribed in eight years. Applying People v. Terrado, it held that the false statements in the 1996, 2004, 2005, and 2006 SALNs were punishable as perjury, which prescribes in ten years, and had prescribed. The Ombudsman reckoned prescription from the dates Gomez omitted the lots from his SALNs, because the titles were registered in his name and registration is notice to the whole world. In its Order dated October 20, 2017 denying both parties' motions for reconsideration, it added, by analogy to PCGG v. Carpio Morales, that prescription runs from the commission of the offense when the data needed to discover it is readily available to the public.

DOF-RIPS filed a Rule 65 petition. It sought additional charges for four counts of perjury, four counts of falsification, and one count of violating RA 3019. It argued that Section 7 of RA 3019 and Section 8 of RA 6713 are separate offenses, that RA 3019 offenses prescribe in 15 years under BP 195, that falsification prescribes in 15 years, and that prescription should run from its discovery of the falsity in 2014 and 2015, when it received the agencies' records. The Ombudsman manifested that it would not participate so as not to advocate for Gomez.
issues: Whether Gomez may be prosecuted for the non-filing of his 2003 SALN under both Section 7 of RA 3019 and Section 8 of RA 6713.
Whether the offense of non-filing of the 2003 SALN had prescribed.
Whether the Ombudsman gravely abused its discretion in ruling that the offenses arising from the false statements in the 1996, 2004, 2005, and 2006 SALNs had prescribed.
Whether prescription of those offenses runs from the filing of the SALNs or from DOF-RIPS's discovery of the falsity.
ruling:
**1. No.** RA 3019 punishes non-filing of the SALN with a fine of P100 to P1,000, imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both. RA 6713 punishes it with imprisonment not exceeding five years, a fine not exceeding P5,000, or both, plus disqualification. Section 16 of RA 6713 expressly repeals or modifies inconsistent laws unless they provide a heavier penalty. Since RA 6713's penalty is heavier, **Section 7 of RA 3019 was amended by Section 8 of RA 6713.** "[N]othing is implied in the repeal," so the rules on implied repeal do not apply. Gomez may not be indicted under both provisions, and the Ombudsman did not gravely abuse its discretion in limiting the charge to RA 6713.

**2. Yes.** Since Gomez can be prosecuted only under RA 6713, the 15-year period under RA 3019 as amended by BP 195 is beside the point. RA 6713 has no prescriptive period of its own, so Act No. 3326 applies. Under Section 1(c), **a violation of Section 8 of RA 6713 prescribes in eight years**, as held in Del Rosario v. People and applied in the Casayuran and Germar cases. The parties disagreed on whether 13 or 11 years had elapsed, but either way the eight-year period had lapsed.

**3. No grave abuse of discretion.** The Constitution and RA 6770 give the Ombudsman wide latitude to determine probable cause, and the Court generally does not interfere. Grave abuse means a capricious or whimsical exercise of judgment amounting to lack of jurisdiction, so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of positive duty. "Disagreement with its findings is not enough." DOF-RIPS showed no specific act or omission of that kind.

**4. From the filing of the SALN.** Following DOF-RIPS v. Ombudsman (Germar), perjury carries a correctional penalty and prescribes in ten years under Article 90. Prescription under Article 91 runs from discovery, but for a SALN, discovery is reckoned from filing. Perjury is consummated upon filing, and the SALN is then subject to review, and "[t]en (10) years is more than enough time to discover any such errors or inaccuracies." This harmonizes the RPC with Section 8(C)(4) of RA 6713, which makes SALNs available to the public for ten years and allows their destruction afterwards unless needed in an ongoing investigation. **Applying this, the discovery of the falsification and perjury is reckoned from the filing of each SALN**, so the false statements in SALNs filed more than ten years before the complaint were barred by prescription.
disposition: The petition was DENIED. The Ombudsman's Resolution dated June 23, 2017 and Order dated October 20, 2017 in OMB-C-C-15-0379 were AFFIRMED.

bar_questions.q: Rodel, a revenue officer, failed to file the SALN due from him in 2011. In 2021, a complaint was filed charging him with violating both Section 7 of RA 3019 and Section 8 of RA 6713 for this omission. The complainant argues that the two are distinct offenses and that RA 3019 offenses prescribe in 15 years. (a) May Rodel be charged under both laws? (b) Has the offense prescribed?

alac.answer: (a) No. Rodel may be charged only under Section 8 of RA 6713. (b) Yes. The offense prescribed in eight years.
alac.legal_basis: Section 16 of RA 6713 expressly repeals or modifies inconsistent laws unless they provide a heavier penalty. Since RA 6713 punishes non-filing of the SALN more heavily than RA 3019, Section 7 of RA 3019 was amended by Section 8 of RA 6713, and an officer cannot be indicted under both. RA 6713 has no prescriptive period, so Act No. 3326 applies. Under Section 1(c), offenses punished by imprisonment of two years or more but less than six years prescribe in eight years. (DOF-RIPS v. Office of the Ombudsman, G.R. No. 236956, November 24, 2021, citing Del Rosario v. People)
alac.application: RA 6713 provides imprisonment of up to five years, a fine of up to P5,000, and disqualification, which is heavier than RA 3019's penalty of up to one year and P1,000. RA 6713 therefore governs, and the express repeal leaves no room for the argument that repeals by implication are disfavored. Since Rodel can be prosecuted only under RA 6713, the 15-year period for RA 3019 offenses is irrelevant. About ten years passed between the 2011 omission and the 2021 complaint, beyond the eight-year period.
alac.conclusion: Rodel can be charged only under RA 6713, and that charge has prescribed.

bar_questions.q: In April 2008, Lina, a customs examiner, filed a SALN that did not declare two lots titled in her name since 2005. In 2020, after a lifestyle check, the complainant obtained certified copies of the titles from the Land Registration Authority and filed a complaint for perjury. It argued that prescription should run only from its discovery of the titles in 2020. Has the crime of perjury prescribed?

alac.answer: Yes. The perjury prescribed ten years after the SALN was filed.
alac.legal_basis: Perjury under Article 183 of the RPC carries a correctional penalty and prescribes in ten years (Art. 90). For false statements in a SALN, the period is reckoned from the filing of the SALN. Perjury is consummated upon filing, the SALN is then subject to review, and Section 8(C)(4) of RA 6713 keeps SALNs available to the public for only ten years. (DOF-RIPS v. Office of the Ombudsman, G.R. No. 236956, November 24, 2021, applying DOF-RIPS v. Ombudsman and Germar, G.R. No. 238660, February 3, 2021)
alac.application: Lina's false SALN was filed in April 2008, so the ten-year period began then and ended in April 2018. The complainant's argument that discovery happened only in 2020 fails because discovery is reckoned from the filing of the SALN, not from when the complainant later gathered records. The complaint filed in 2020 came after the period had run.
alac.conclusion: The perjury charge against Lina is barred by prescription.

bar_questions.q: The Ombudsman dismissed some counts of a complaint filed by a government agency against a public employee on the ground of prescription, explaining its computation in detail. The agency filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 65 with the Supreme Court, arguing only that the Ombudsman's computation was wrong and that the Court should substitute its own reading of the evidence. Will the petition prosper?

alac.answer: No. Mere disagreement with the Ombudsman's findings is not grave abuse of discretion.
alac.legal_basis: The Constitution and RA 6770 give the Ombudsman wide latitude in its investigatory and prosecutorial powers, and the Court generally does not interfere with its determination of probable cause. Its acts are reviewable on certiorari only for grave abuse of discretion, meaning a capricious or whimsical exercise of judgment equivalent to lack of jurisdiction, so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of positive duty. Disagreement with its findings is not enough. (DOF-RIPS v. Office of the Ombudsman, G.R. No. 236956, November 24, 2021)
alac.application: The agency points to no arbitrary, despotic, or whimsical act by the Ombudsman. It only says the Ombudsman reached a different conclusion on prescription. The Ombudsman's ruling was reasoned and followed the governing law and jurisprudence, so there is no basis for the extraordinary writ.
alac.conclusion: The petition for certiorari should be dismissed for failure to show grave abuse of discretion.

notes: The decision gives two filing dates for the DOF-RIPS complaint: August 28, 2015 in the facts and September 1, 2015 in the last part of the ruling. The Court did not squarely resolve DOF-RIPS's argument that falsification of public documents prescribes in 15 years. It held that the Ombudsman, which had treated the false SALN statements as perjury under People v. Terrado, committed no grave abuse of discretion, and it reckoned both the falsification and the perjury from the filing of the SALNs. The Ombudsman's charges for the 2007-2009 SALNs were not at issue. The index title contains a garbled character in "DOF-RIPS"; it is corrected in full_title.
